summary: Defines a Uniform Resource Name namespace that lets Object Identifiers (the dotted numbers used to name things in ASN.1 and similar systems) be written as URNs. This gives those numbers a standard, location-independent text form. It was replaced by RFC 3061.

plainLanguage.summary: Some things are named with long strings of numbers separated by dots. This gives those number names a standard way to be written like web-style names. A newer note later replaced it.

questions: how to write an object identifier as a urn
how to write oid as urn
subtitle: Encoding Object Identifiers as Uniform Resource Names.

tldr.problem: Object Identifiers (OIDs) are a way to name things in ASN.1 systems and network management, but they are long numbers with dots and are not URI-style names, which is inconvenient for modern network protocols.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the "oid" URN namespace that lets people write Object Identifiers as uniform resource names (URNs) in a standard, consistent way, like urn:oid:1.3.6.1.
tldr.outcome: This namespace specification was replaced by RFC 3061 as the OID URN approach evolved, but the core idea of giving OIDs a standard URI form remains useful.

today: RFC 3001 is obsolete and replaced by RFC 3061. However, the urn:oid namespace remains a standard way to write Object Identifiers as URIs for use in modern protocols.

sections.title: What Are Object Identifiers?
sections.content:
An Object Identifier (OID) is a series of numbers separated by dots, such as 1.3.6.1 or 1.3.6.1.4.1. They are defined in ASN.1 and are used for naming things in network management, directory services, and cryptography. Once an entity is assigned an OID, that entity can create new OIDs under it (subdelegation).

The top three levels are pre-assigned: 0 is for ITU-T, 1 is for ISO, and 2 is for joint ISO/ITU-T assignments. Important OIDs include 1.3.6.1 (the Internet OID) and 1.3.6.1.4.1 (IANA-assigned company OIDs used in network management).
sections.plainLanguage: Some things in computer networks have names that are just numbers with dots, like 1.3.6.1.4.1. These are called Object Identifiers, and people use them in management systems.

sections.title: The OID URN Namespace
sections.content:
RFC 3001 defines the "oid" URN namespace so that Object Identifiers can be written as Uniform Resource Names in a standard way. An OID like 1.3.6.1.4.1 becomes urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1. The namespace specification uses the string encoding rules from RFC 1778, which require digits separated by periods with the most significant digit on the left.

The namespace guarantees uniqueness and persistence: OIDs cannot be reused once assigned, and by reference, the URN namespace inherits those rules. This means urn:oid identifiers are guaranteed to be permanent and unique.
sections.plainLanguage: By writing OID numbers in a URN (web-style name), they can be used in modern Internet protocols and look like regular web names instead of just dots and numbers.

sections.title: Examples and Use
sections.content:
The RFC provides examples: urn:oid:1.3.6.1 is the Internet OID, urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1 is for private company MIBs, urn:oid:1.3.6.1.2.1.27 is the Applications MIB, and urn:oid:0.9.2342.19200300.100.4 represents an object class from the X.500 directory pilot project.

The namespace is global and formal. At the time of this RFC, no central resolution mechanism was defined (you cannot look up urn:oid names the way you can look up domain names), but the URN form provides a standard way to reference OIDs in specifications and protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Here are some examples of how to write real OIDs as URNs: urn:oid:1.3.6.1 for the Internet, urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1 for companies. They look like web addresses but are actually OID numbers.
